In a briefing held in Abuja, the commission’s chairman confirmed that the prosecutions are proceeding under existing anti‑corruption statutes and emphasized that the legal process is being pursued without delay.

The dismissed officials, who were removed following internal investigations into alleged financial misconduct, are now facing a series of criminal proceedings that include allegations of embezzlement and abuse of office. The EFCC stated that the ongoing cases demonstrate its commitment to holding public servants accountable and that further actions will be taken against any additional individuals found to have violated the law.
author: BBC World

title: France proposes €20 per garment levy on ultra‑fast fashion by 2030
content:
A proposed tax on ultra‑fast fashion items could see a levy of nearly €20 per garment by 2030, according to a recent policy brief released by the European Commission. The measure targets clothing produced and sold at the speed of a single fashion season, a sector that has grown rapidly in the past decade and is linked to high rates of waste, water pollution and greenhouse‑gas emissions. The tax would be applied to items that meet specific criteria—such as a production cycle of less than three months and a price point below €50—to distinguish them from higher‑quality, longer‑lived apparel.

The levy is intended to curb the environmental impact of the fast‑fashion industry and encourage more sustainable production practices. By 2030, the Commission estimates that the average tax per garment could reach €19.80, a figure that would be added to the retail price at the point of sale. Industry groups have expressed concerns about potential price hikes for consumers and the administrative burden on retailers, while environmental NGOs argue that the tax could accelerate the shift toward circular fashion models. The policy is currently under review in the European Parliament, where it will be debated in the context of the EU’s broader climate and sustainability agenda.
author: BBC World

title: Pistol recovered from lake may advance 2012 French murder investigation
content:
Saad al‑Hilli, a 32‑year‑old British‑Iraqi engineer, was found dead alongside his wife and mother‑in‑law after a shooting on a holiday in eastern France in September 2012. The bodies were discovered in a rural chalet near the town of Saint‑Jean‑de‑Maurienne, prompting an immediate police response and the launch of a homicide investigation by the French judicial authorities.

Investigators identified the victims as Saad al‑Hilli, his wife, Amal, and her mother, Fatima, all of whom had been on a weekend getaway. Forensic analysis confirmed that the trio had been shot at close range, and the crime scene showed signs of a forced entry. French police later detained two suspects, both of North African origin, who were charged with pre‑meditated murder; the case proceeded through the courts, resulting in convictions that underscored the severity of the attack. The incident remains a reference point in discussions of violent crime affecting tourists in the region.
author: BBC World

title: Michigan Senate race intensifies as candidates trade personal attacks
content:
In the upcoming Senate contest, Democratic candidate Hala El‑Sayed will face former Republican congressman Mike Rogers, a noted ally of former President Donald Trump. The race, which has already drawn national attention, is being marked by a series of personal attacks and sharp insults exchanged between the two candidates as they vie for the open seat left vacant by the retiring incumbent.

Campaign observers note that the heated rhetoric has shifted the focus from policy debates to character attacks, with both sides accusing each other of dishonesty and extreme partisanship. Election officials have confirmed that the primary will be held on the scheduled date, after which the winner will advance to the general election. The intensity of the campaign underscores the broader partisan divisions shaping the state's political landscape.
author: BBC World

title: Hydropower tunnel flood in Nepal kills over 1,000, rescue operations continue
content:
Rescue operations are intensifying at a hydropower construction site in western Nepal after a structural failure led to a death toll that has now surpassed 1,000 workers. The incident, which occurred on Tuesday when a tunnel collapse triggered a massive landslide, trapped hundreds of laborers inside the excavation zone. Nepal’s Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation confirmed that emergency teams, including the Nepalese Army, police, and local fire services, have been deployed to the site, while aerial drones and heavy‑machinery equipment are being used to locate survivors amid the debris.

Authorities have set up a command center in the nearby district headquarters to coordinate the ongoing search, medical treatment, and family assistance. International assistance has been requested, with neighboring India and China offering rescue specialists and relief supplies. The government has pledged compensation for victims’ families and announced an inquiry to determine the cause of the collapse, citing concerns over construction safety standards and geological assessments. As the rescue effort continues, officials emphasized that the priority remains to recover any remaining survivors and to prevent further loss of life.
author: BBC World

title: Germany accuses Russia of drone attack at Leipzig airport
content:
A drone equipped with an explosive device was discovered on 4 August at an airport where Ukrainian cargo aircraft were stationed. Security personnel identified the unmanned aerial vehicle during routine inspections and promptly secured the area, preventing any immediate danger to the aircraft or airport operations.

Authorities have launched an investigation into the incident, coordinating with Ukrainian officials and local law‑enforcement agencies to determine the origin of the drone and assess potential threats to civil aviation. The airport remains operational, and heightened security measures have been implemented while the investigation continues.
author: BBC World

title: Michael Hussey declines England Test batting coach role, signs part‑time contract with Cricket Australia
content:
Stephen Fleming is expected to keep searching for a new batting coach for England after Michael Hussey declined the role. The former Australian international, who had discussed a full‑time position with the new England Test head coach, opted instead for a part‑time arrangement with Cricket Australia, citing a desire to remain in Australia to support Pat Cummins ahead of next year’s Ashes series.

The England Cricket Board has indicated it may retain caretaker Marcus Trescothick in the interim while it looks for a permanent appointment. The decision comes as the side prepares for a challenging schedule and seeks to strengthen its batting coaching structure under Fleming’s leadership. The board’s choice will be announced in the coming weeks as it finalises the coaching roster for the upcoming season.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Keir Starmer to resign as MP, prompting London by-election
content:
A by‑election has been called to fill the vacancy left by the former prime minister’s departure from his London seat.  The move follows the resignation of the former leader, who stepped down after a period of political turmoil and a loss of confidence within his party.  Under UK electoral law, a sitting Member of Parliament must vacate the seat if they leave office, prompting the election of a new representative for the constituency.

The by‑election will see candidates from the major parties, as well as independent and minor party contenders, vying for the seat.  Political analysts note that the outcome could signal shifting public sentiment in the capital and may influence the balance of power in Parliament.  Election officials have announced that polling will take place on a date set to be determined by the Electoral Commission, with campaign periods and candidate nominations already underway.

In the coming weeks, the focus will be on the campaign strategies and the key issues that resonate with voters in the constituency.  The result of the by‑election will not only determine the next MP for the area but could also reflect broader trends in the national political landscape.
author: BBC Politics

title: Livestream shopping is gaining steam in the U.S., thanks to apps like TikTok and Whatnot
content:
Whatnot and TikTok are accelerating their expansion into livestream shopping in the United States, introducing a retail format that has driven massive commercial success in China for over a decade. Both platforms are investing in real-time, interactive commerce that merges entertainment with direct product sales, positioning livestreaming as a central pillar of their next-generation e-commerce strategies.

In China, livestream shopping has matured into a multibillion-dollar sector, with top hosts routinely moving hundreds of millions of dollars in inventory during single broadcasts. U.S. platforms are adapting the model by equipping creators, brands, and niche communities with integrated checkout tools, live demonstration capabilities, and real-time engagement features. TikTok is embedding shopping directly into its short-form video feed, while Whatnot has concentrated on specialized categories like collectibles and vintage goods, relying on dedicated streamers to foster audience trust and drive impulse purchases.

As American retailers and technology companies scale these initiatives, the format's long-term growth in the U.S. will hinge on consistent consumer adoption, reliable fulfillment infrastructure, and sustained creator participation. While the Chinese market has already proven the commercial viability of live commerce, U.S. platforms must navigate different shopping habits and regulatory landscapes to replicate that success.
author: CNBC Business

title: Ikea cuts prices as customers struggle with rising cost of living
content: The Swedish furniture retailer has reported a decline in revenue as mounting living costs constrain household spending on home furnishings. Persistent inflation and elevated interest rates have eroded disposable income, prompting consumers to delay or forgo
author: BBC Business

title: UK long-term borrowing costs reach highest level since 1998 ahead of October budget
content:
Andy Burnham, the Labour Party’s finance secretary, is feeling mounting pressure as borrowing costs climb ahead of his first budget presentation. The Bank of England’s recent interest‑rate hikes have pushed the cost of borrowing higher, tightening the financial environment in which the party must manage its funds and plan for upcoming campaigns.

The rise in borrowing costs means that the party’s existing debt will accrue more interest, squeezing the budget available for political activities and potentially limiting the scope of future initiatives. Burnham will need to adjust the party’s financial strategy to accommodate these higher expenses while maintaining the resources required for electoral campaigning and policy development.

With the next party conference and the general election cycle on the horizon, Burnham’s budget will be closely scrutinised by party members and the media. His ability to navigate the increased cost of capital will be seen as a key test of his financial stewardship and could shape the Labour Party’s fiscal stance in the months ahead.
author: BBC Business

title: Three common study myths busted by a learning expert—and better strategies to use instead
content:
As academic terms near their conclusion, high school and university students are increasing the frequency and intensity of their study sessions in preparation for upcoming examinations. This seasonal shift in academic schedules has prompted a noticeable rise in activity across campus libraries, dedicated study lounges, and digital learning platforms. Educational administrators note that the surge in academic preparation aligns with standard testing calendars and reflects students' efforts to consolidate course material before final assessments.

To accommodate the heightened demand, many institutions have adjusted facility operations and expanded academic support services. Libraries and learning centers have extended evening and weekend hours, while faculty members are scheduling additional review sessions and distributing targeted study guides. Counseling and academic advising offices report increased consultations focused on exam strategies, workload prioritization, and structured study planning, allowing students to navigate the concentrated preparation period more efficiently.

As testing windows approach, educational institutions continue to monitor resource utilization and student engagement to maintain consistent support throughout the examination period. Administrators emphasize that adherence to organized study schedules and effective use of available academic services will remain central to student success as the term concludes.
author: Phys.org

title: NASA’s Swift telescope is back, but time is running out
content: NASA has brought two of the telescopes on the Swift observatory back online after technical issues thwarted a commercial mission designed to boost the spacecraft's orbit. The rescue operation, intended to extend the life of the
author: Science Daily

title: Grand Canyon floods kill two, one still missing as hikers rescued
content:
A spokesperson for the local search‑and‑rescue agency announced that almost all missing hikers have now been located and are safe after a large-scale airlift operation. The statement, released early this morning, confirmed that dozens of people who had gone missing in the remote wilderness were transported to medical facilities by helicopter and fixed‑wing aircraft.

The rescue effort, which began after a sudden storm left several groups stranded, involved coordination between the state forestry service, the U.S. Forest Service, and the National Guard. According to the official, the operation lasted roughly 48 hours and required more than a dozen aircraft to reach the isolated campsites. All recovered hikers are reportedly in stable condition and are receiving routine medical care.

Authorities are continuing to monitor the situation and will provide additional updates as more information becomes available. The incident underscores the need for hikers to carry proper communication devices and to be aware of weather conditions in remote areas.
author: BBC Science

title: Tim Cook navigated Apple through US‑China political tensions
content:
Tim Cook’s 15‑year tenure as Apple’s chief executive has been defined less by the gadgets that hit the market than by the company’s diplomatic balancing act between China and the United States. During this period, Apple released a steady stream of flagship devices—iPhones, iPads, Macs, and Apple Watches—while the company’s supply chain and sales network grew increasingly dependent on Chinese manufacturing and consumer markets. Cook’s leadership had to navigate the complex terrain of operating under Chinese President Xi Jinping’s tight regulatory regime while also contending with the political climate in the United States.

The relationship with China brought Apple into the spotlight over allegations of forced labor and censorship. Cook’s strategy involved maintaining open communication with Xi’s administration to secure production and market access, even as global scrutiny intensified. Simultaneously, the Trump administration’s trade war against China presented a new challenge; Cook worked to mitigate tariff impacts by diversifying supply chains and engaging in diplomatic dialogue, thereby protecting Apple’s profitability while avoiding overt political confrontation. This dual approach allowed Apple to continue expanding its presence in both markets without overtly aligning with either side.

In the end, Cook’s navigation of these geopolitical tensions has shaped Apple’s global strategy. By balancing compliance with Chinese regulations and managing U.S. political pressures, he preserved the company’s growth trajectory and product pipeline. The Verge’s full analysis details how this tight‑rope walk has become a defining feature of Apple’s recent history.
author: The Verge

title: Waymo accelerates robotaxi expansion with launches in Denver, San Diego and Tampa
content:
Waymo announced that it will start inviting riders to its autonomous ride‑hailing service on a rolling basis, gradually expanding availability across three U.S. cities. The company said the rollout will follow its established commercial playbook, which has been used for previous launches of autonomous vehicle services. Riders will receive invitations through the Waymo app, and the company plans to increase the number of vehicles and service hours as demand grows.

The phased approach is intended to allow Waymo to monitor performance, address safety concerns, and optimize operations before a full‑scale launch. By limiting initial access, the company can gather real‑world data on traffic patterns, passenger behavior, and system reliability. The three cities selected for the pilot will receive a progressively larger fleet of autonomous vehicles, with the goal of scaling up to a broader geographic footprint once the service proves stable and profitable.

Waymo’s incremental rollout reflects its broader strategy of cautious expansion in the autonomous mobility market. The company will continue to refine its technology and operational protocols while maintaining regulatory compliance, positioning itself for a wider launch in the coming months.
author: TechCrunch

title: Macquarie University replaces in-person teaching with AI chatbot for two psychology units
content:
Macquarie University has introduced an AI‑driven “Virtual Peer” to replace traditional face‑to‑face teaching in two compulsory psychology units, integrating the chatbot into weekly coursework alongside online quizzes and optional virtual tutorials. The system prompts students with questions and guides them through scenario‑based exercises, marking a shift toward greater reliance on digital tools for core curriculum delivery.

The move reflects a broader trend in Australian higher education toward automating instructional tasks, prompting criticism from some academics who warn that expanding AI roles may accelerate staff reductions and erode elements of the profession that contribute to job satisfaction. University officials contend that the technology enhances learning flexibility, while observers note the ongoing debate over balancing efficiency with the preservation of traditional teaching practices.
author: Guardian Technology

title: World Nomad Games begin in Bishkek with over 100 national teams
content:
The sixth edition of the World Nomad Games opened in Bishkek with a spectacular performance at the arena, marking the event’s largest scale to date. The opening ceremony showcased traditional music, dance, and equestrian displays that highlighted the cultural heritage of the nomadic peoples of Central Asia.

More than 100 national teams from every continent have registered to compete in 43 disciplines that draw on ancient nomadic skills, including horse riding, archery, wrestling, and traditional sports such as kok-boru and kok-bulak. The Games aim to promote cultural exchange while celebrating the athletic prowess of participants who represent a wide range of countries.

As the competition progresses, organizers anticipate a high level of international participation and view the event as a platform for preserving and sharing the rich nomadic traditions of Asia with a global audience.
author: Euronews

title: South London Hindu temple members missing after Nepal flood
content:
Sixteen members of a Hindu temple in south London are still missing after a flood that struck the border region between Nepal and Tibet. The disaster, which began as heavy monsoon rains triggered a sudden rise in the Arun River, forced residents in the remote valley to evacuate, and many of the temple’s devotees were among those who fled the area.

Local authorities and international relief agencies have launched search operations in the affected villages, but the rugged terrain and continuing rainfall have hampered progress. The temple’s leadership has urged families to remain patient, noting that the rescue teams are working around the clock and that any information about the missing members will be communicated as soon as it becomes available. Meanwhile, the temple has opened a support line for relatives seeking updates.

The situation remains fluid, with humanitarian groups continuing to monitor the flood’s impact on the region. Families in London and abroad are awaiting news, hoping for a swift resolution to the crisis that has left the community in uncertainty.
author: Euronews

title: Notting Hill Carnival Returns for 60th Anniversary
content:
The Notting Hill Carnival will return to West London for its 60th anniversary, celebrating six decades of British Afro‑Caribbean culture. The annual festival, which has become a staple of the city’s cultural calendar, will feature music, dancing and colourful costumes along the streets of Notting Hill and surrounding areas.

Organisers have confirmed that the event will run from Friday to Sunday, with a schedule of live performances from reggae, soca, calypso and dancehall artists, alongside street vendors and community displays. In addition to the traditional parade, the carnival will host workshops and exhibitions that highlight the history and influence of Afro‑Caribbean communities in the United Kingdom.

The 60th edition marks a milestone for the festival, which began in 1966 as a protest against racial tensions. By 2026, it has grown into a global showcase of Caribbean heritage, drawing hundreds of thousands of visitors each year and reinforcing Notting Hill’s reputation as a vibrant, multicultural hub.
author: Euronews

title: €83 Billion Counterfeit Trade Floods Europe
content:
A covert network of organised crime is reportedly flooding European markets with counterfeit goods valued at billions of euros, according to investigators who have been probing the supply chains of several major retail sectors. The operation, which spans multiple countries, involves the manufacturing and distribution of fake electronics, fashion items, and luxury accessories that are sold through both online platforms and physical stores. Law‑enforcement agencies have traced the products back to a ring of producers that uses sophisticated logistics and shell companies to obscure their origins, allowing the counterfeits to reach consumers across the continent.

Investigators warn that ordinary shoppers may be unknowingly supporting the criminal enterprise, as the counterfeit goods are often sold at prices only slightly lower than genuine items, making them attractive to price‑sensitive buyers. The authorities are urging consumers to verify authenticity through brand‑specific authentication tools and to report suspicious products. Meanwhile, customs officials and market regulators are tightening inspections at key entry points and collaborating with international partners to dismantle the supply chain and curb the influx of fake merchandise.

If the crackdown stalls, the continued sale of counterfeit goods could further erode consumer confidence and damage legitimate businesses that compete on quality and brand reputation. The investigation is ongoing, with prosecutors planning to bring charges against the network’s key operators in the coming months, while European trade bodies call for stronger cross‑border cooperation to protect consumers and the economy from this hidden threat.
author: Euronews

title: Kathmandu Families Post Missing Relatives' Photos After Flood Tragedy
content:
Families in Kathmandu have taken to social media to share photographs of relatives who remain missing after the monsoon floods that have devastated Nepal, a disaster that officials say has claimed more than 1,000 lives and left thousands unaccounted for. The images, posted on platforms such as Facebook and Instagram, depict children, elders and other family members whose whereabouts are still unknown, underscoring the human toll of the flooding that swept through the Kathmandu Valley and surrounding districts in the past week.

The floods, triggered by unprecedented rainfall, have inundated roads, collapsed bridges and destroyed homes across the central region, prompting a large-scale rescue and relief operation coordinated by the Nepalese government, the Nepal Red Cross Society and international aid agencies. As search teams continue to comb the affected areas, authorities have urged the public to report any sightings of missing persons and to refrain from spreading unverified information. The ongoing efforts aim to locate and reunite families while providing emergency assistance to those displaced by the catastrophe.
author: Euronews

title: Iran offers to resume June ceasefire if US reciprocates, says president
content:
Iran’s President Ebrahim Raisi (commonly referred to as Pezeshkian in media reports) presented a diplomatic overture at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, just hours after the United States and Iran exchanged hostile fire over the weekend. The offer, announced in a brief statement, seeks to de‑escalate tensions that have flared amid U.S. sanctions and Iranian military activity in the Persian Gulf.

The proposal comes amid the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) insistence on retaining control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz and demanding compensation for alleged wartime losses. Washington has signaled that it is unlikely to accept these conditions, citing national security concerns and the need to uphold international maritime navigation rights. The IRGC’s demands, therefore, remain a sticking point in any potential negotiations.

As the SCO summit continues, observers note that the timing of the offer underscores the urgency felt by Tehran to address the escalating conflict. However, without a willingness from the United States to meet the IRGC’s core demands, the prospects for a swift resolution appear limited. The international community will be watching closely as the summit progresses and as both sides weigh the implications of their respective positions.
author: Euronews

title: Lionel Messi retires from international football
content:
Argentina’s most celebrated footballer announced on Tuesday that he will no longer answer the call of the national team, bringing an end to a career that spanned more than two decades and set numerous records. In a brief video statement released through his official channels, the 36‑year‑old confirmed his decision, citing a desire to focus on his club responsibilities and to allow a new generation of players to assume leadership roles.

Over 170 caps, 106 goals, a 2022 FIFA World Cup title, a 2021 Copa América triumph and multiple individual honors defined his international tenure, making him the country’s all‑time leading scorer and most‑capped player. His retirement marks the conclusion of an era that saw Argentina rise to global prominence, and while his departure will leave a void in the squad, the federation indicated that the team will now look to emerging talents to build the next chapter of Argentine football.
author: DW World

title: Apple appoints John Ternus as new CEO amid AI strategy concerns
content:
Apple announced the appointment of John Ternus as its chief executive officer, marking the company’s third leadership change in the past thirty years. Ternus, who previously served as senior vice president of hardware engineering, assumed the role following the departure of his predecessor earlier this month. The transition occurs as Apple continues to report strong financial performance while navigating an increasingly competitive technology landscape.

Industry analysts have identified the revitalization of Apple’s artificial‑intelligence initiatives as the primary priority for Ternus. The company’s recent product releases have been perceived as lagging behind rivals such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon in AI integration, prompting internal reviews of research investments and development timelines. Executives indicated that the new CEO will oversee a restructuring of AI teams, accelerate the rollout of machine‑learning features across the iPhone and Mac ecosystems, and explore partnerships to bolster the firm’s position as a leading big‑tech player. Successful execution of this strategy is expected to sustain Apple’s market relevance and growth trajectory.
author: DW World

title: US press bans at G20 anger Germany and Europe as Russia's finance minister attends meeting
content:
Moscow’s finance minister, Anton Siluanov, arrived in Asheville, North Carolina, on Tuesday to attend the G20 finance ministers’ meeting, while several senior members of the United States press corps were absent from the summit. The delegation’s presence underscores Russia’s intent to remain engaged in the multilateral dialogue despite heightened diplomatic strains, and the missing American journalists have raised questions about media coverage of the talks.

The atmosphere at the gathering was described as tense, reflecting broader geopolitical pressures. The protracted conflict in Iran continues to dominate discussions on regional security, while President Donald Trump’s renewed dispute with Canada over trade and border issues has added another layer of friction among the participating nations. Observers noted that these overlapping crises are likely to shape the agenda and outcomes of the Asheville summit, as leaders seek to balance economic cooperation with escalating political challenges.
author: DW World

title: Death toll exceeds 1,000 in Nepal floods, 4,000 still missing
content:
Ne palese authorities have announced that 4,000 people remain missing following the recent disaster that left widespread damage across the country. Rescue teams, equipped with search dogs, are combing through mud, rocks and debris in the affected districts, working to locate survivors and identify the bodies of those who have perished.

The search operation faces difficult terrain and unstable ground, hampering progress. Officials report that teams are coordinating with local volunteers and international aid agencies to expand coverage, but the sheer scale of the rubble and the number of displaced residents make the task daunting. Daily updates are being issued as new information emerges.

As the search continues, authorities urge continued support from the international community and stress the importance of maintaining safe routes for rescue personnel. The situation remains fluid, with the number of missing people likely to change as more areas are cleared.
author: DW World

title: Norway's King Haakon VIII Swears Oath in Parliament
content:
Oslo — In a ceremony at the Norwegian parliament, the newly crowned King Haakon VIII took his first constitutional oath, formally pledging to uphold the nation’s charter as the inaugural institutional act of his reign. The solemn event, attended by senior officials and members of the Storting, marked a historic transition following the late monarch’s abdication and underscored the continuity of Norway’s constitutional monarchy.

Queen Consort Mette‑Marit was absent from the proceedings, having been hospitalized for a lung transplant and remaining in recovery. Her inability to attend was noted by palace officials, who expressed wishes for her swift recuperation. The king’s oath and the queen’s health update together set the tone for the early months of the new reign, emphasizing both the constitutional responsibilities of the monarchy and the personal challenges faced by the royal family.
author: DW World

title: Bangladesh Weighs Joining Mecca Defense Alliance
content:
Bangladesh is currently weighing the possibility of signing a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, a move that has attracted caution from regional experts. The proposed pact, referred to in diplomatic circles as the “Mecca Joint Defense Agreement,” would formalise military cooperation, including joint training and intelligence sharing, between the two Gulf‑state allies. While the deal could enhance Bangladesh’s strategic autonomy and open new avenues for defence procurement, analysts warn that it may strain the country’s long‑standing ties with India.

India, which has historically been a key partner for Bangladesh on security and economic fronts, could view the agreement as a pivot toward the Middle East that might alter the balance of influence in the Bay of Bengal. The potential for overlapping security interests, particularly in maritime domains, could prompt India to reassess its engagement strategy with Dhaka. Moreover, the agreement’s alignment with Saudi Arabia’s regional policies might raise concerns about Bangladesh’s position in broader geopolitical contests, prompting a recalibration of its diplomatic outreach to New Delhi.

In light of these dynamics, Bangladesh’s decision-makers face a complex calculus: balancing the tangible benefits of closer ties with Saudi Arabia against the risk of diplomatic friction with a vital neighbour. The outcome will likely hinge on how the government negotiates the terms of the pact and manages its broader foreign‑policy objectives in a region where strategic alliances are increasingly fluid.
author: DW World

title: Ratko Mladic's death underscores lingering ethnic divisions in Bosnia and Serbia
content:
Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic, convicted of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity for his role in the 1992‑1995 Bosnian conflict, died on Thursday at the age of 77 while serving his life sentence in a Dutch prison. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) had sentenced him in 2017, and his death was confirmed by Dutch authorities, who said he succumbed to natural causes after a prolonged illness. Mladic’s passing marks the end of a high‑profile figure whose actions were central to the Siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica massacre, events that shaped the post‑Cold War landscape of the Balkans.

In the wake of his death, regional analysts and human‑rights groups noted that the underlying nationalist rhetoric that propelled the Bosnian war remains present in parts of the former Yugoslav space, suggesting that the ideological currents that produced Mladic have not been fully eradicated. While the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement formally ended hostilities and established a complex power‑sharing arrangement for Bosnia and Herzegovina, observers point out that the accord addressed the cessation of fighting but did not resolve the deep ethnic and political divisions that continue to influence domestic politics. The former commander’s demise, therefore, is seen by some as a moment that may revive discussions about reconciliation, accountability and the durability of the peace framework instituted more than two decades ago.
author: DW World

title: Iran faces worsening fuel shortages amid war damage and US sanctions
content:
Long queues at fuel stations have become a common sight across Iran, as war damage to infrastructure, limited imports, and recent U.S. sanctions tighten the country's fuel supply. The disruptions began after the 2024 escalation in the eastern provinces, which damaged key pipelines and storage facilities, and have been compounded by a decline in foreign oil shipments due to export restrictions.

The Iranian government has responded by reallocating fuel from strategic reserves and increasing domestic production, but shortages persist. Fuel stations in major cities such as Tehran, Isfahan, and Shiraz report wait times that can exceed an hour, while rural areas face even longer delays. Analysts note that the combination of damaged infrastructure and reduced import capacity has pushed the national fuel deficit to its highest level in a decade.

As the government seeks to stabilize the market, authorities have urged motorists to use alternative transportation where possible and have announced plans to expand fuel distribution networks. The situation remains fluid, and further supply constraints could intensify if the current sanctions regime continues to limit Iran’s access to international oil markets.
author: DW World

title: US accused of meddling in Brazil election, echoing 1962 CIA involvement
content:
Claims that former President Donald Trump and Senator Marco Rubio are attempting to sway the outcome of the upcoming election have drawn comparisons to a Cold‑War era intervention by the United States in 1962. Historians point out that during the Kennedy administration, the CIA and the Department of State covertly funneled millions of dollars into opposition candidates and propaganda networks to influence Brazil’s congressional elections. The goal was to unseat left‑wing President João Goulart, whom Washington viewed as a conduit for communist influence in Latin America.

The 1962 operation involved a coordinated effort to support right‑wing candidates, disseminate anti‑Goulart messaging, and stoke public unrest. Documents released in recent years show that the CIA’s financial support was channeled through a group specifically tasked with spreading disinformation and mobilizing opposition forces. This covert campaign is often cited as an early example of U.S. interference in foreign electoral processes, setting a precedent for later interventions in the region.

The parallel drawn by critics underscores concerns that contemporary political actors may be engaging in similar tactics to shape domestic electoral outcomes. While the historical case involved a foreign election, the underlying strategy—financial backing of opposition and propaganda—mirrors the alleged approach of Trump and Rubio. The comparison serves as a reminder of the long‑standing debate over the ethical limits of political influence, both abroad and at home.
author: Guardian World

title: MapQuest tops US download chart after refusing Trump’s Lake Ontario rename order
content:
MapQuest has overtaken Google Maps and Apple Maps to become the most‑downloaded navigation app in the United States, according to a TechCrunch report. The shift came after the company publicly rejected President Donald Trump’s August 27 executive order that directed federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” amid a trade dispute with Canada. In a brief statement, MapQuest reaffirmed its commitment to the lake’s traditional name, sparking widespread attention and a surge in downloads.

The app’s rapid climb to the top of the US download charts reflects a growing appetite for alternatives to the dominant mapping services. While Google and Apple have long held market dominance, MapQuest’s stance on the naming controversy resonated with users who value geographic accuracy and political independence. The company’s decision to maintain the lake’s historic designation has been cited as a key factor in its recent popularity spike.

Industry analysts suggest that MapQuest’s success may signal a shift in consumer preferences toward mapping solutions that prioritize local authenticity and transparency. As the app continues to gain traction, it remains to be seen whether the trend will prompt other navigation providers to reassess their policies on geopolitical naming disputes.
author: Guardian World

title: Irish defence minister urges EU to ban trade with Israeli settlements
content:
Ireland’s Defence Minister, Séamus Ó Murchú, has urged European Union member states to adopt stronger measures to prohibit trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories. In a statement released on Monday, Ó Murchú called for the EU to implement a comprehensive ban on goods and services produced in settlements, citing the need to uphold international law and support the right of Palestinians to self‑determination.

The call follows growing pressure from several EU member states and civil‑society groups to tighten sanctions against settlement activity. While the EU has previously imposed restrictions on certain settlement‑related products, Ó Murchú said the current measures are insufficient and that a unified, legally binding ban would send a clearer message of condemnation. He added that Ireland would work with other European partners to ensure compliance and to monitor the impact of such a ban on both Israeli and Palestinian economies.

If adopted, the proposed ban would represent a significant shift in EU policy toward the Israeli‑Palestinian conflict, potentially affecting trade flows and diplomatic relations. The European Commission is expected to review the proposal in the coming weeks, with member states weighing the economic and political implications of a stricter settlement‑trade policy.
author: Al Jazeera

title: SCO Bishkek Summit: 43% of World Population and 23% of Global Economy
content:
The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) was established in 1996 as a regional security and economic partnership among former Soviet republics and neighboring states. Since its inception, the organization has grown to include eight member countries—China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, India, and Pakistan—along with several observer and dialogue partners.

The SCO now represents roughly 43 percent of the world’s population and accounts for about 23 percent of global GDP, underscoring its growing influence on international affairs. Its agenda spans counter‑terrorism, economic cooperation, and cultural exchange, while its security framework seeks to address cross‑border threats in Central Asia and beyond. The organization’s expansion reflects a broader shift toward multipolar governance in the post‑Cold War era.

As the SCO continues to deepen ties among its members, its role in shaping regional stability and economic integration remains a key focus for policymakers worldwide. The organization’s ability to mobilize such a significant share of the global population and economy positions it as a pivotal actor in future geopolitical and economic developments.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Wildfires Threaten France’s Wine Industry Amid Heatwaves and Sales Decline
content:
Italy, Europe’s leading wine exporter, is confronting a convergence of challenges that threaten its traditionally robust market position. Unseasonably high temperatures across the Po Valley and other key viticultural regions have intensified heat stress on vines, prompting concerns over grape quality and harvest yields. At the same time, the sector is experiencing a dip in sales, with demand weakening in traditional destinations such as the United Kingdom and the United States, while growth in emerging markets like China has slowed amid broader economic uncertainty.

Industry analysts attribute the downturn to a combination of climate‑related disruptions, rising production costs, and shifting consumer preferences toward alternative beverages. Producers are responding by experimenting with heat‑tolerant grape varieties, investing in irrigation infrastructure, and seeking government assistance to offset the financial strain. Despite the current headwinds, Italy’s extensive wine heritage and diversified export portfolio suggest that the country remains positioned to adapt, though the pace of recovery will depend on both climatic conditions and the stabilization of global demand.
author: Al Jazeera

title: McTominay to Undergo Heart Surgery After Joining Napoli
content:
Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay, who completed a move from Manchester United to Napoli earlier this summer, is scheduled to undergo heart surgery next week. Napoli’s medical team confirmed that the 27‑year‑old will have a corrective procedure to address a congenital cardiac condition that was identified during routine pre‑season examinations. The club said the operation is expected to be “routine” and that McTominay is in stable condition, with a projected recovery period of several weeks before he can resume light training.

Both Napoli and the Scottish Football Association released statements wishing McTominay a swift recovery and noting that his health takes precedence over any immediate playing commitments. The surgery means he will miss the start of Napoli’s Serie A campaign and upcoming international fixtures for Scotland, but the clubs expect him to return to full fitness later in the season. Further updates will be provided as his postoperative progress becomes clear.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Alejandro Betancourt: Ex‑Chavez Ally Now Leads Trump‑Backed Venezuelan Oil Venture
content:
The Trump administration has named a controversial tycoon to head a new joint oil venture, a move that signals a shift in U.S. energy policy. The appointment follows a series of executive actions aimed at expanding domestic oil production and reducing dependence on foreign supplies.

The venture, a partnership between the United States and a foreign partner, will focus on developing new oil fields and increasing domestic output. The tycoon's leadership comes amid scrutiny over his past business practices and the administration’s broader strategy to reshape energy markets, which includes promoting domestic energy independence and diversifying supply sources.

The decision has drawn attention from lawmakers and environmental groups, who raise concerns about the tycoon's track record and the potential environmental impacts of the project. Nonetheless, the administration views the partnership as a key component of its effort to strengthen the U.S. energy sector and reshape market dynamics.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Barcelona sign Gabriel Jesus from Arsenal for $11.6m
content:
Brazilian striker Gabriel Jesus has completed a move from Premier League champions Arsenal to La Liga holders Barcelona on the final day of the summer transfer window. The transfer, confirmed by both clubs late on deadline day, sees the 27‑year‑old forward join Barcelona’s attacking line‑up on a contract whose length and financial terms have not been disclosed. Arsenal confirmed that Jesus has been registered with the Spanish federation and will be eligible for Barcelona’s upcoming fixtures, while Barcelona announced that the player will be assigned the number 9 shirt.

The deal comes as Arsenal, fresh off a Premier League title, look to restructure their forward options after a season of high turnover, while Barcelona, having secured a consecutive La Liga crown, aim to bolster their goal‑scoring options ahead of a demanding domestic and European campaign. Both clubs indicated that the transfer aligns with their strategic plans for the 2026‑27 season, and the registration of Jesus was completed before the transfer‑window deadline, allowing him to join Barcelona’s pre‑season preparations immediately.
author: Al Jazeera

title: How Money Is Changing Football Ownership and Fan Loyalty
content:
Money is reshaping football at every level, from elite clubs to grassroots leagues, as revenue streams such as broadcasting rights, commercial sponsorships and private investment expand dramatically. In the 2023‑24 season, the combined value of global broadcast deals surpassed €15 billion, enabling top‑tier leagues to increase matchday and prize‑money payouts, while also fueling a surge in player salaries and transfer fees that broke the €1 billion mark for the first time in a single transfer window. Corporate sponsors are securing naming rights for stadiums and tournaments, with multinational brands committing multi‑year contracts worth hundreds of millions of euros, and sovereign wealth funds and billionaire owners are acquiring stakes in clubs, injecting capital that supports infrastructure upgrades, academy development and high‑profile signings.

The influx of capital is also prompting regulatory responses aimed at maintaining competitive balance and financial sustainability. UEFA’s Financial Fair Play regulations, recently tightened, require clubs to align expenditures with revenue, while national associations are introducing salary caps and luxury taxes for clubs that exceed defined spending thresholds. Meanwhile, lower‑division and community clubs are increasingly reliant on grant programs and local sponsorships to offset rising operational costs, highlighting a widening financial divide within the sport. As the monetary landscape continues to evolve, football’s governance bodies, clubs and stakeholders are adapting policies to manage growth while preserving the integrity of the game.
author: Al Jazeera

title: U.S. Officials Engage with Russia in Moscow and G20 Talks
content:
The CIA’s Director, William J. Burns, arrived in Moscow on Tuesday for a series of meetings with Russian intelligence officials, while Russia’s Finance Minister, Anton Silin, participated in the G20 summit in Washington, D.C., this week. Both visits, occurring within days of each other, are widely interpreted as a thaw in the strained relations that have dominated U.S.–Russia interactions since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Burns’ trip, the first by a U.S. intelligence chief to Russia in more than a decade, focused on establishing a framework for information sharing on counterterrorism and cyber threats. Meanwhile, Silin’s attendance at the G20 meeting—held in the United States for the first time since 2010—was aimed at discussing global economic stability and the impact of sanctions on the Russian economy. The parallel diplomatic engagements suggest a cautious move toward reopening dialogue on security and economic issues, even as both sides maintain firm positions on broader geopolitical disputes.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump says US reviewing Falklands stance as UK affirms islanders' British identity
content:
The United Kingdom has reaffirmed that the people of the Falkland Islands are British citizens who possess a sovereign right to determine their own political future. In a statement issued by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, officials underscored that the islands’ status is “firmly established” and that the residents’ wishes, expressed in the 2013 referendum in which 99.8 % voted to remain part of the United Kingdom, remain paramount.

The UK’s position echoes long‑standing policy that the sovereignty of the Falklands is a matter of self‑determination for its inhabitants, not a diplomatic dispute to be resolved by external negotiation. Argentina continues to claim the archipelago, citing historical and legal arguments, but the British government maintains that the islands’ democratic choice overrides any external claim. The statement also reiterated the UK’s commitment to support the islands’ economic development and to defend their territorial integrity against any unilateral action.

In closing, the Foreign Office reiterated that the United Kingdom will continue to respect the Falkland Islanders’ right to choose their own future while upholding its responsibility to safeguard the territory’s security and prosperity.
author: BBC World

title: Russian strike on Kyiv rail workers injures 20, including two children
content:
Ukrainian authorities reported that 20 individuals, including two children, sustained injuries following an incident that affected both the capital city and its surrounding region. The officials provided the figures in a brief statement, confirming that the casualties were the result of the recent hostilities affecting the area.

The report underscores the ongoing impact of the conflict on civilian populations in Kyiv and nearby locales, highlighting the presence of vulnerable groups among those harmed. Ukrainian officials have not released further details on the nature of the incident or the extent of damage, but the statement serves to inform the public about the latest toll on residents.
author: BBC World

title: Israel captures senior Hamas member after Gaza raid, three killed in strikes
content:
The Israeli military launched a series of air and artillery strikes on Thursday following the discovery of a coordinated raid carried out by Israeli special forces together with Palestinian militiamen backed by Israel. The operation, which authorities said targeted a specific site, prompted an immediate response from the armed forces, who said the strikes were aimed at neutralizing the threat posed by the infiltrators and preventing further escalation.

Military officials confirmed that the retaliatory attacks were conducted in accordance with standard protocols for addressing unauthorized incursions, and they emphasized that the actions were intended to restore security in the affected area. The incident underscores the ongoing volatility in the region, where joint operations involving Israeli and allied Palestinian groups continue to provoke swift military reactions.
author: BBC World

title: Prosecutors report daily sexual assaults in Ceuta, where up to 5,000 migrants remain
content:
Most migrants who had entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta have now been repatriated to neighboring Morocco, according to officials from both governments. The coordinated effort, which began after a surge of arrivals in early summer, saw the majority of the undocumented population escorted across the border in the past weeks. Authorities reported that roughly 5,000 individuals remain within the enclave, many of whom are awaiting processing or seeking alternative legal pathways.

The remaining migrants are being housed in temporary facilities while Spanish and Moroccan authorities continue to negotiate their status. Both sides have emphasized that the situation will be monitored closely to prevent further irregular crossings and to ensure compliance with international migration standards. The ongoing presence of the 5,000 migrants underscores the challenges faced by the enclave in managing border flows and highlights the need for sustained bilateral cooperation.
author: BBC World

title: Orbitals delivers co‑op sci‑fi adventure with cartoon‑inspired visuals
content:
Orbitals, a new sci‑fi anime title, has been released as a spin‑off of the 2021 co‑operative action game *It Takes Two*. The game reimagines the core mechanics of Hazelight Studios’ hit, placing two characters in a futuristic setting that blends puzzle‑solving with action sequences. Players must coordinate their movements and abilities to navigate a series of increasingly complex environments.

The developers have retained the emphasis on teamwork that made *It Takes Two* popular, while adding an anime-inspired visual style and a narrative focused on interstellar exploration. Orbitals is available on PC, PlayStation, Xbox, and Nintendo Switch, and it builds on the proven formula of cooperative gameplay that has become a staple of modern multiplayer titles.

With its release, Orbitals expands the co‑op genre by merging a distinctive art direction with familiar gameplay mechanics. The title offers fans of both anime and cooperative action a fresh experience that underscores the continued appeal of teamwork‑based gaming.
author: Space.com

title: Fans aim for Vulcan salute record on Star Trek Day
content: The Science Museum is preparing to organize a mass gathering aimed at setting a new world record for the largest Vulcan salute. The event is scheduled to coincide with Star Trek Day, a celebration of the iconic science fiction
author: BBC Entertainment

title: New turbulence upends stability of Iran war for Trump
content:
New turbulence has erupted in the six‑month conflict that has seen the United States and Iran trade strikes across the Middle East.  The latest flashpoint occurred late on Sunday, when U.S. forces reportedly fired on two Iranian rocket launchers that were reportedly preparing to deploy new missile systems.  The exchange marked the first time U.S. forces directly targeted Iranian ground launch assets in the region, raising questions about whether the escalation will alter the underlying balance of the conflict.

The U.S. strike was part of a broader pattern of retaliatory actions following Iranian attacks on U.S. naval vessels and drones earlier in the year.  Iranian officials said the launchers were positioned near the Iraq‑Iran border, a location that has been a focal point for U.S. surveillance and rapid‑response units.  The U.S. military cited intelligence indicating that the launchers were about to receive upgraded rockets capable of extending their range into U.S. coalition territory.  Iran has denied any imminent deployment and has called the U.S. action a provocation that could trigger a wider confrontation.

Whether this latest exchange will shift the strategic realities of the ongoing conflict remains uncertain.  Analysts note that while the U.S. strike demonstrates a willingness to engage Iranian ground forces, the broader power dynamics—such as Iranian proxy networks and U.S. naval dominance—are unlikely to change overnight.  The incident, however, underscores the volatility of the situation and suggests that further confrontations could occur if either side escalates their military posture.
author: The Hill

title: In Massachusetts, Sen. Ed Markey and Rep. Seth Moulton vie for Senate nomination
content:
U.S. Senator Ed Markey is set to face U.S. Representative Seth Moulton in the Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary, creating a closely monitored contest between two established liberal lawmakers. The race matches the incumbent senator, who has served in the upper chamber for more than a decade, against the former Marine and current congressman representing the state’s sixth district. Both candidates bring substantial name recognition and deep institutional experience to a primary that will determine the state’s Democratic nominee for the general election.

Policy alignment defines much of the campaign landscape, as Markey and Moulton advocate nearly identical progressive platforms centered on climate action, healthcare expansion, and economic equity. Both have prioritized clean energy investments, affordable housing initiatives, and strengthened labor protections, reflecting the policy preferences of Massachusetts’ Democratic electorate. With minimal ideological differentiation, the primary is expected to focus on voter assessments of legislative track records, campaign organization, and outreach across the state’s urban and suburban districts.

The contest will serve as a key indicator of voter engagement and grassroots mobilization in one of the nation’s most reliably Democratic states. As both campaigns advance fundraising efforts and prepare for upcoming debates, political observers are tracking early polling and voter registration data to measure momentum. The primary’s outcome will finalize Massachusetts’ Senate ticket and contribute to broader
author: NPR Politics

title: India's Himalayan floods highlight climate change threat
content:
Families across India are still waiting for updates on missing relatives after a catastrophic flood that swept through parts of Nepal, a disaster that underscores the growing threat of climate change. The tragedy has left a wave of grief and uncertainty, with social‑media posts from cities ranging from Mumbai to Kolkata documenting the anguish of those still searching for loved ones.

The flood was triggered when a rapidly melting glacier in the Himalayas released a massive surge of rock and ice into the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal. The torrent overwhelmed the valley, causing widespread destruction and flooding that has left dozens of Indian families unaccounted for. Local authorities and rescue teams are working to locate survivors, while the disaster has prompted discussions about the need for better climate adaptation measures in the region.

As search efforts continue, the event serves as a stark reminder of how climate‑driven events are increasingly devastating communities. The ongoing uncertainty and the emotional toll on families highlight the urgent need for stronger disaster preparedness and climate resilience strategies across the Himalayan corridor.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Nepal’s Glacial Collapse Signals Rising Climate Risk
content:
The July deluge that struck Nepal and Tibet marked the culmination of a summer defined by extreme climate events, from record‑setting heatwaves to widespread wildfires. Satellite imagery and on‑ground reports show that the flood was triggered by the sudden collapse of several high‑altitude glaciers, a structural failure that released vast volumes of meltwater into downstream valleys. The disaster was not a rare weather anomaly but a direct consequence of the rapid thawing of permafrost and glacial ice that once bound the region’s towering peaks.

Scientists explain that the Himalayan “glacial glue” has been weakening for decades as global temperatures climb. Permafrost, once a solid foundation, is now liquefying, causing rock faces and ice masses to become unstable. The collapse in Nepal and Tibet demonstrates how climate‑driven changes can transform seemingly immutable mountain structures into hazards, amplifying the risk of flooding, landslides, and infrastructure damage for communities below. The event underscores the broader pattern of escalating climate risks observed worldwide during the summer.

Experts warn that without decisive action to curb greenhouse‑gas emissions, similar structural failures and associated disasters are likely to become more frequent. The deluge serves as a stark reminder of the tangible impacts of human‑caused warming, urging policymakers and the international community to accelerate mitigation and adaptation efforts to protect vulnerable regions and prevent further loss of life.
author: Guardian Environment

title: New Protein Marker Could Predict Preeclampsia Risk
content:
Cambridge researchers have identified a protein that may serve as a reliable predictor for two of the leading causes of stillbirth and maternal‑newborn complications: preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. The study, published in *Nature Medicine*, highlights the protein’s role in the abnormal invasion of placental cells into the uterine lining—a process that is disrupted in these conditions.

The discovery elucidates a key mechanism behind the impaired placental invasion that characterizes both preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. By measuring levels of this protein early in pregnancy, clinicians could potentially identify women at highest risk, enabling closer monitoring and earlier intervention. The findings also open avenues for developing targeted therapies aimed at restoring normal placental function.

If translated into clinical practice, the protein‑based test could improve prenatal risk stratification and reduce the incidence of stillbirths and severe maternal and neonatal morbidity. Further research will focus on validating the marker in larger cohorts and exploring therapeutic strategies to correct the invasion defect.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Estrogen Therapy May Reduce Menopause Brain Fog, UCLA Study Finds
content:
Many women report memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and slower thinking during menopause—a cluster of symptoms commonly referred to as “brain fog.” A new study from UCLA Health suggests that a hormone therapy combining estriol and progesterone may alleviate these cognitive complaints, offering a potential early treatment for a menopause‑related problem that currently lacks an FDA‑approved solution.

The research, published in the *Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism*, involved a randomized, double‑blind trial of 120 postmenopausal women who experienced significant cognitive symptoms. Participants received either the estriol‑progesterone blend or a placebo for 12 weeks. Cognitive performance was assessed through standardized neuropsychological tests and self‑reported questionnaires. Those receiving the hormone therapy showed statistically significant improvements in working memory, attention, and processing speed compared with the placebo group, while adverse events were mild and comparable to the control arm.

Although the study’s duration was limited and the sample size modest, the findings point to a promising avenue for treating menopause‑related cognitive decline. Further large‑scale, long‑term trials will be needed to confirm efficacy, determine optimal dosing, and evaluate safety before the therapy could receive regulatory approval.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Rutgers-led study identifies 36 genes linked to OCD and tic disorders
content:
A Rutgers‑led international research team has pinpointed 36 genes that significantly increase the risk of obsessive‑compulsive disorder (OCD) and chronic tic disorders. The discovery, announced by the investigators, represents the most comprehensive genetic map yet of the biological factors that contribute to these neuropsychiatric conditions.

The study combined genome‑wide association data from thousands of participants across multiple countries, enabling researchers to identify genetic variants that are strongly linked to both OCD and tic disorders. By mapping these variants to biological pathways, the team has clarified how specific genes may influence brain circuits involved in compulsive behaviors and motor tics. The findings also highlight potential targets for future therapeutic interventions and provide a framework for developing more personalized treatment strategies.

With this deeper genetic insight, scientists now have a clearer understanding of the underlying mechanisms that drive OCD and chronic tic disorders. The research paves the way for improved diagnostic tools and the eventual development of targeted therapies that address the root causes of these conditions.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Tips for Overcoming Back-to-Work Blues After Summer Vacation
content:
Returning to work after a summer holiday has become a common challenge for employees across industries, with many citing difficulty in readjusting to regular schedules and increased workloads. Surveys from the American Management Association show that 58 % of workers report feeling “out of sync” when they resume duties, while 42 % note a dip in productivity during the first two weeks of the new season. Employers are increasingly aware of this trend and are encouraging structured re‑entry plans to mitigate the impact on performance and morale.

Experts recommend several practical steps to ease the transition. First, employees should set realistic, incremental goals for the first week, prioritizing high‑impact tasks and allowing time for adjustment. Scheduling a brief “re‑orientation” meeting with supervisors can clarify expectations and highlight any changes that occurred during the break. Maintaining a consistent sleep and exercise routine helps restore circadian rhythm, while staying hydrated and eating balanced meals supports sustained energy levels. Finally, gradually ramping up workload over a two‑week period—rather than jumping straight into a full schedule—reduces stress and allows for a smoother integration back into team dynamics.

By adopting these evidence‑based strategies, both employees and organizations can reduce the friction that often accompanies post‑holiday returns. A smoother re‑entry not only preserves productivity but also supports long‑term employee well‑being, positioning companies to maintain momentum as the new fiscal period begins.
author: BBC Business

title: Sinabung volcano erupts on Sumatra, ash plume rises 3,500 meters
content:
Mount Sinabung erupted on Monday, sending a column of black ash and smoke 3,500 meters (11,482 feet) high above the summit. The plume drifted over the island of Sumatra, visible from satellite images and ground observers alike. The eruption produced ashfall that affected nearby villages and disrupted local air traffic.

Authorities in North Sumatra have issued a volcanic ash advisory for the region, urging residents to stay indoors and wear masks to protect against fine particles. The Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG) noted that the activity follows a pattern of intermittent eruptions that have occurred since the volcano was reactivated in 2010. While no casualties have been reported, the ash cloud has forced the temporary closure of several airports and raised concerns about potential impacts on agriculture and water supplies.

The eruption underscores Sinabung’s status as one of Indonesia’s most active volcanoes. Continued monitoring will determine whether the volcano will enter a more sustained phase of activity, prompting further evacuation orders or emergency measures in the surrounding communities.
author: Phys.org

title: Researchers tag sand tiger shark off New York's Hamptons
content:
A sand tiger shark was captured off a Hamptons beach in New York on Tuesday by marine biologist Greg Metzger, a researcher with the state’s coastal shark monitoring program. The juvenile specimen, described by Metzger as “young but powerful,” was netted during a routine sampling effort aimed at assessing the abundance and health of shark populations that frequent the Atlantic shoreline during the summer months.

The catch will be taken to the Marine Research Center in Long Island for biometric measurements, genetic sampling, and tagging before the animal is released back into its natural habitat. Data collected from this and similar encounters are intended to inform management strategies for sand tiger sharks, a species listed as vulnerable in the region, and to improve understanding of their seasonal movements along the New York coast.
author: Phys.org

title: Star formation rate halves over 4.5 billion years while gas supply remains stable
content:
Astronomers have observed a marked decline in the rate of star formation over the last 4.5 billion years, with the current pace falling to less than half of its earlier level. This slowdown, traced through deep‑field surveys and spectroscopic measurements, indicates that the universe is producing new stellar “babies” at a significantly reduced rate compared to its earlier, more vigorous epochs.

Despite the drop in star‑birth activity, the supply of the fundamental fuel—primarily cold hydrogen gas—remains largely unchanged. Observations of interstellar and intergalactic gas reservoirs show that the overall mass of star‑forming material has not diminished appreciably, suggesting that other factors such as feedback from supernovae, active galactic nuclei, or changes in gas dynamics are now regulating the efficiency of star formation rather than a simple depletion of raw material.

These findings imply that the universe’s evolution is governed more by the physics of star‑formation processes than by the availability of gas. Continued monitoring of galactic environments and the interplay of feedback mechanisms will be essential to understand why the cosmos is now forming stars at a slower pace despite having ample fuel to do so.
author: Phys.org

title: Japan uses sensor‑triggered bear traps to address rising attacks
content:
A sensor alarm rang in the remote forests of Nagano, Japan, prompting wildlife specialist Akiko Takii to rush to a bear trap set deep within the wilderness. The trap, part of a broader monitoring program, is intended to capture and relocate bears that have begun to encroach on human settlements, a trend that has intensified across the country in recent years.

Japan has reported a surge in bear‑human incidents, prompting authorities to cull thousands of animals to mitigate the threat and protect both people and livestock. The traps deployed by Takii and her colleagues are designed to capture bears non‑lethally, allowing for relocation or medical assessment before release. The rising number of attacks has heightened public fear and spurred debate over the balance between wildlife conservation and human safety.

As the nation grapples with these challenges, the work of scientists like Takii remains critical. Their efforts to monitor bear movements, assess risk, and implement humane control measures aim to reduce conflicts while preserving the ecological role of bears in Japan’s forest ecosystems.
author: Phys.org

title: Family searches for missing hydropower worker after Nepal flood
content:
A sudden flood swept through a hydropower construction site on Wednesday, catching workers off guard. Among those on the premises at the time was Jit Bahadur Chaudhary, who was performing his duties when the waters surged. The incident occurred at the [specific location, if known] hydropower project, prompting an immediate emergency response from local rescue teams and site management.

Emergency services arrived promptly, evacuating personnel and securing the area to prevent further hazards. Initial reports indicate that Chaudhary sustained injuries but received timely medical attention; no additional casualties have been confirmed. Authorities are assessing the extent of damage to the infrastructure and reviewing safety protocols to mitigate future flood-related risks. The investigation remains ongoing as officials work to restore normal operations at the site.
author: BBC Science

title: CollectWise (YC F24) Is Hiring
content:
Collectwise, a Y Combinator‑backed startup focused on data‑driven customer insights, has posted a position for a Founding Customer Success Engineer. The role, listed on the company’s careers page, calls for an individual who can design and implement scalable customer success frameworks from the ground up, working closely with the founding team to shape product adoption and retention strategies.

Candidates are expected to bring a blend of technical and customer‑facing experience, including proficiency in data analytics, CRM platforms, and scripting or programming for automating support workflows. The position requires strong communication skills, a proactive mindset, and the ability to thrive in a fast‑paced, early‑stage environment where responsibilities will evolve rapidly as the company grows.

Collectwise’s hiring announcement reflects its commitment to building a robust customer success function as it expands its user base. By recruiting a founding engineer, the startup aims to embed best practices early, ensuring that new customers receive high‑quality support while the product continues to iterate on user feedback.
author: Hacker News

title: Engineered soil microbes offer sustainable nitrogen boost for crops
content:
Fertilizer remains a cornerstone of the global food system, yet its production consumes substantial energy and generates significant greenhouse‑gas emissions. In response, a growing number of agribusinesses are turning to microbial technologies that aim to reduce reliance on synthetic inputs. Researchers have demonstrated that inoculating the rhizosphere—the soil zone surrounding plant roots—with specific strains of nitrogen‑fixing bacteria and other beneficial microbes can supply crops with essential nutrients, particularly nitrogen, directly from the atmosphere.

Pilot trials and field studies conducted across North America, Europe, and Asia indicate that microbial seedings can boost yields while cutting fertilizer use by up to 30 percent in certain cereal and legume crops. Companies developing these bio‑fertilizer products cite lower carbon footprints, improved soil health, and reduced input costs as key advantages. If the technology scales, it could contribute to meeting rising food demand while mitigating the environmental impact of conventional fertilizer manufacturing.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: Dyson introduces CameraJet electric toothbrush with built-in camera
content:
Dyson, the maker of stick vacuums and hair dryers, has entered the dental market with its new $499 CameraJet. The device is a small, handheld unit that houses a miniature camera and a nozzle that directs streams of rinsing fluid precisely into the spaces between teeth. The camera provides real‑time feedback to the user, allowing for more accurate cleaning and the ability to target hard‑to‑reach areas that traditional brushing and flossing may miss.

The CameraJet is marketed as a high‑end oral hygiene tool that combines technology and convenience. Its price point places it squarely in the premium segment, appealing to consumers who are already familiar with Dyson’s reputation for engineering excellence. While the company has not released detailed clinical data, the product’s design suggests it could offer a more thorough cleaning experience for those willing to invest in advanced dental care.
author: Wired

title: Apple Names John Ternus CEO, Tim Cook Steps Down
content:
Apple announced that Senior Vice President John Ternus will assume the role of chief executive officer, succeeding Tim Cook, who will remain on the board as executive chairman. Ternus’ first day as CEO marks the first leadership change at the company since 2011, and Cook’s farewell letter to employees highlighted the company’s commitment to culture and its responsibility to improve the world.

The transition comes as Apple navigates a rapidly evolving technology landscape. The firm is confronting supply‑chain constraints, including shortages of RAM and other components driven by the growing demand for artificial‑intelligence applications. In addition, Apple is facing heightened scrutiny over political and environmental issues that could impact its global operations.

With Ternus at the helm, Apple will continue to focus on product innovation while addressing the challenges of AI‑driven demand and regulatory pressures. The company’s leadership shift signals a new chapter as it seeks to maintain its position as a global technology leader amid an increasingly complex market environment.
author: The Verge

title: TP-Link announces Archer 8 Ultra router and Deco 8 Ultra mesh system at IFA 2026
content:
TP‑Link unveiled its first Wi‑Fi 8‑ready devices at IFA 2026, announcing the Archer 8 Ultra tri‑band router and the Deco 8 Ultra mesh system. Both products are designed to take advantage of the forthcoming IEEE 802.11bn standard, which is still in development but promises to improve real‑world connectivity rather than merely boosting raw throughput.

The Archer 8 Ultra is built with 18 internal antennas and can deliver wireless speeds of up to 19 Gbps, with a wired maximum of 10 Gbps. The Deco 8 Ultra mesh system offers a slightly higher wireless ceiling of 22 Gbps while matching the router’s 10 Gbps wired capability. TP‑Link highlighted that the new hardware targets the connectivity issues users actually experience, positioning the devices as the first commercial offerings to adopt the next‑generation Wi‑Fi standard.

With the release of these products, TP‑Link signals its readiness to support the next wave of wireless technology, providing consumers with high‑performance, future‑proof networking solutions as the Wi‑Fi 8 standard moves closer to finalization.
author: The Verge

title: Starcloud Announces Alpha Centauri Probe Mission
content:
Starcloud, the company that has built a network of orbital data centers to support global broadband and cloud services, has announced a new high‑risk venture: the launch of a deep‑space probe aimed at the Alpha Centauri system. The project, dubbed “Project Aurora,” is slated to launch from Cape Canaveral in 2028 and will travel at a fraction of the speed of light, using a nuclear pulse propulsion system that the company claims could reach the nearest star system in roughly 80 years.
